extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (appellants, patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evaluative standards governing when an examiner's answer on appeal constitutes a 'new ground of rejection', how it must be presented/approved, appellant response options and timing, and the petition process to challenge or obtain reopening of prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a new ground of rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Any new ground of rejection made by an examiner in an answer must be: (A) approved by a Technology Center (TC) Director or designee; and (B) prominently identified in the 'Grounds of Rejection to be Reviewed on Appeal' section under the subheading 'New Grounds of Rejection'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner may use form paragraph 12.256. The examiner’s answer must provide appellant a two-month time period for reply. The examiner may use form paragraph 12.279.01 to notify appellant of the period for reply and to include the approval of the TC Director or designee. All new grounds of rejection must be approved by a TC Director or designee (see MPEP § 1207.03 and related notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellant's two options when an examiner’s answer contains a new ground of rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If an examiner's answer contains a rejection designated as a new ground of rejection, appellant must within two months from the date of the examiner's answer either: (1) reopen prosecution by filing a reply under 37 CFR 1.111 with or without amendment, affidavit or other evidence relevant to the new ground; or (2) maintain the appeal by filing a reply brief under 37 CFR 41.41 addressing each new ground of rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any amendment, affidavit or other evidence filed with a reply brief will be treated as a request to reopen prosecution under 37 CFR 41.39(b)(1). A reply brief under 37 CFR 41.41 must address each new ground as set forth in 37 CFR 41.37(c)(1)(iv) and should comply with other requirements of 37 CFR 41.37(c). Extensions of time under 37 CFR 1.136(a) do not apply to the TWO MONTH period; see 37 CFR 1.136(b) and 1.550(c) for extendability in patent and reexamination proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: When citation/application of evidence in an examiner's answer requires designation as a new ground
rubrics_metrics.description: If Evidence (such as a new prior art reference, but not including a newly relied upon dictionary definition) is applied or cited for the first time in an examiner’s answer, then 37 CFR 41.39(a)(2) requires that the rejection be designated as a new ground of rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the citation of a new prior art reference is necessary to support the rejection, it must be included in the statement of rejection and be designated as a new ground. See MPEP § 1207.03 discussion and MPEP § 1204.04 for what constitutes 'evidence' for appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change in 'basic thrust of the rejection' triggers new ground
rubrics_metrics.description: A position or rationale that changes the 'basic thrust of the rejection' will give rise to a new ground of rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (In re Kronig, 539 F.2d 1300) establishes that whether the thrust changed is fact-specific; however, merely using different language or restating the reasoning in a different way does not necessarily create a new ground if the basic thrust remains the same (see In re Kronig, In re Jung, In re Noznick, In re Krammes, In re Cowles). The controlling criterion is whether appellants have had a fair opportunity to react to the thrust of the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not permissible: using a new ground to reject previously allowed or objected-to claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A new ground of rejection would not be permitted to reject a previously allowed or objected to claim even if the new ground would rely upon evidence already of record; rather, the examiner should reopen prosecution in such instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the basis for the new ground was approved by a supervisory patent examiner as set forth in MPEP § 1207.04, the examiner would reopen prosecution rather than make a new ground in the answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: changing statutory basis from 35 U.S.C. 102 to 35 U.S.C. 103 constitutes a new ground
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner’s answer changes the statutory basis of the rejection from 35 U.S.C. 102 to 35 U.S.C. 103, then the rejection should be designated as a new ground of rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court in In re Hughes held that such a change constitutes a new ground because issues under the two statutes may be 'vastly different' and require different types of evidence and opportunity to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: changing statutory basis from 103 to 102 based on different teaching constitutes a new ground
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner’s answer changes the statutory basis of the rejection from 35 U.S.C. 103 to 35 U.S.C. 102 and relies on a different portion of a reference going beyond the previously relied-upon portion, the rejection should be designated as a new ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Echerd — appellants should have opportunity to present rebuttal evidence as to new assumptions of inherent characteristics when the board/examiner relies on different portions/teachings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: citing new calculations for overlapping ranges constitutes a new ground
rubrics_metrics.description: If a rejection is based upon range values or calculations first presented in the examiner’s answer (e.g., overlapping ranges, particle sizes), the rejection should be designated as a new ground of rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Kumar: Board reliance on appendix calculations not found by examiner constituted a new ground because Board found facts not found by examiner, requiring opportunity for response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: relying on different structure in support of structural obviousness constitutes a new ground
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner’s answer relies on a different structure than previously relied upon to support an obviousness rejection based on structural similarity, then the rejection should be designated as a new ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Wiechert: when rejection is factually based on an entirely different portion of an existing reference, the appellant must be afforded opportunity to respond as to that portion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: pointing to a different portion of the claim to maintain a 'new matter' 35 U.S.C. 112 rejection constitutes a new ground
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner’s answer identifies a different feature or aspect of the rejected claim as constituting 'new matter' (e.g., relying on a numerical limitation not previously alleged), the rejection should be designated as a new ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Waymouth: Board affirmed on a wholly different basis than the examiner (different alleged new matter), which required a new ground designation because it necessitated different responses by appellants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situations that do NOT constitute a new ground — general principle
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no new ground of rejection when the basic thrust of the rejection remains the same such that an appellant has been given a fair opportunity to react to the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where statutory basis and evidence relied upon remain the same, changes in discussion or rationale do not necessarily create a new ground. See In re Kronig and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-new-ground example: citing a different portion of a reference that merely elaborates on previously cited teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner’s answer cites a different portion of an applied reference which goes no farther than, and merely elaborates upon, what was taught in the previously cited portion, then the rejection does not constitute a new ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re DBC: Board citing an Example that merely elaborated on the same generic limitations cited earlier did not create a new ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-new-ground example: changing statutory basis but relying on same teachings
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing the statutory basis of rejection (e.g., 103 to 102) does not constitute a new ground if it relies on the same teachings of the remaining reference(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re May: court affirmed under 102 because it relied on the same prior-art species as both examiner and Board — 'lack of novelty is the epitome of obviousness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-new-ground example: relying on fewer references but same teachings
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner’s answer removes one or more references from a 103 rejection but relies on the same teachings of the remaining references, the change does not constitute a new ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Kronig: Board limited discussion to fewer references but relied on same teachings — not a new ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-new-ground example: changing order of combining references but relying on same teachings
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing the order of references in a 103 rejection does not create a new ground if the same teachings are relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Cowles and In re Krammes support that different order of combining references, without change in teachings, is not a new ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-new-ground example: examiner responding to applicant-submitted reference by pointing to other portions of that same reference
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant submits a reference and the examiner's answer points to other portions of that same reference to counter applicant's argument, this ordinarily does not constitute a new ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Hedges: Solicitor searched references of record for disclosures pertinent to applicant's arguments — not a new ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure to petition Director under 37 CFR 41.40 (petition to designate new ground and reopen prosecution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any request to seek review of the primary examiner's failure to designate a rejection as a new ground of rejection must be by petition to the Director under 37 CFR 1.181 filed within two months from the entry of the examiner's answer and before the filing of any reply brief; failure to timely file constitutes a waiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If petition is granted, prosecution reopens and appellant gets a two-month period to file a reply under 37 CFR 1.111; if petition is denied, appellant may file a single reply brief under 37 CFR 41.41. A reply brief filed after petition filing but before decision withdraws the petition and maintains the appeal. Authority to decide delegated to TC Director or designee. Time periods are not extendable under 1.136(a) but may be under 1.136(b) or 1.550(c). No corrected examiner’s answer will be provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellant cannot request reopening under 37 CFR 41.39(b) unless rejection designated as new ground
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellant cannot request to reopen prosecution pursuant to 37 CFR 41.39(b) if the examiner’s answer does not have a rejection that is designated as a new ground of rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To seek reopening when the examiner fails to designate what appellant believes is a new ground, appellant must use the petition procedure under 37 CFR 41.40 (petition to Director under 1.181).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of failing to timely respond to an examiner’s answer containing a new ground
rubrics_metrics.description: If appellant fails to timely file a reply under 37 CFR 1.111 or a reply brief within the two-month period required by 37 CFR 41.39, the appeal as to the claims subject to the new ground of rejection is dismissed and those claims are canceled; only remaining claims continue and the application will be forwarded to the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP provides form paragraph guidance to insert claim numbers and mailing dates when informing appellant of dismissal and remaining claims. See MPEP ¶ 12.279.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing/extendability rules for reply periods
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner’s answer must provide appellant a two-month time period for reply to a new ground of rejection; extensions under 37 CFR 1.136(a) are not applicable to this two-month period, but extensions may be available under 37 CFR 1.136(b) for patent applications and 37 CFR 1.550(c) for ex parte reexamination proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two-month period is critical for avoiding sua sponte dismissal as to the claims subject to the new ground. See 37 CFR 41.39(b) and related MPEP paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervisory approval required to reopen prosecution after an appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must obtain supervisory approval in order to reopen prosecution after an appeal; see MPEP §§ 1002.02(d) and 1207.04.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reopening prosecution is necessary rather than making a new ground in the examiner’s answer, supervisory approval is required prior to reopening.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a newly cited reference may not constitute a new ground (exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a newly cited reference is added merely as evidence of what the examiner previously stated was 'well-known' in the art and that statement was challenged for the first time in the appeal brief, the citation of the reference in the examiner’s answer would not ordinarily constitute a new ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2144.03 and related discussion — the key is that the new citation merely supports an earlier-stated, challenged proposition rather than introducing a new substantive ground requiring rebuttal evidence.
